subtopics.title: Demographic Winter: Meaning and Key Indicators
subtopics.summary: Demographic winter is a persistent and structural decline in population growth, and it is no longer limited to developed countries. Its key indicators are fertility below the replacement level of 2.1 and an inverted population pyramid with a rising old-age dependency ratio. It can lead to a shrinking workforce, a rising fiscal burden from ageing and a potential loss of the demographic dividend.
facts: Demographic winter: a persistent and structural decline in population growth.
Now a global phenomenon, not limited to developed countries.
Fertility rate below replacement level of 2.1 children per woman.
Inverted population pyramid: shrinking young population and expanding elderly population.
Rising old-age dependency ratio is a key indicator.
Demographic dividend: growth potential from a larger working-age population compared to dependents.
Total fertility rate (TFR) is the average births per woman; 2.1 is the replacement level.
Fertility refers to children born to a woman during reproductive years (ages 15-49).

subtopics.title: Causes and Negative Impacts of Demographic Winter
subtopics.summary: Causes include delayed life milestones, urbanisation, societal and cultural shifts, and greater access to family planning. A declining population brings a shrinking workforce, pressure on pension and healthcare systems, and greater isolation of the elderly. Developed nation trends suggest that a rebound is unlikely once fertility falls below the replacement level.
facts: Delayed milestones: later marriages and parenthood due to career priorities, economic insecurity and high housing and education costs.
Urbanisation: smaller and costlier urban housing discourages larger families.
Societal shifts: greater female workforce participation, preference for smaller families and changing family norms.
Access to family planning gives greater reproductive autonomy and reduces unintended births.
Shrinking workforce threatens future labour supply as youth replacement falls short over time.
Ageing population raises the burden on healthcare, elderly care and pension systems.
Low-fertility states face youth shortages; high-fertility states struggle with overpopulation.
Smaller families disrupt traditional support systems, leading to greater elderly isolation.
Declining fertility and late marriages are linked to social isolation and mental health challenges.
Developed nation trends show that a rebound is unlikely once rates fall below replacement level.

subtopics.title: China's Birth Control Policy: Timeline
subtopics.summary: China's approach moved from birth control being a minor priority under Mao Zedong to a central policy push in the 1970s. The One-Child Policy (1980) restricted most couples to a single child, and it was later replaced by a Two-Child Policy and a Three-Child Policy (2021). Fertility rates did not rebound despite these relaxations.
facts: Pre-1970s (Mao Zedong era): birth control existed but was not a major policy priority.
Great Leap Forward (1958-62) aimed to boost production and living standards but resulted in famine and millions of deaths.
Population growth rebounded after the Great Leap Forward was rolled back.
1970s five-year plans promoted birth control, often through coercive measures.
Slogan 'Later, Longer, Fewer' encouraged delayed marriages, longer intervals between births and fewer children.
One-Child Policy (1980) formally restricted most couples to a single child.
The One-Child Policy aimed to curb rapid population growth and ease pressure on resources.
Three-Child Policy introduced in 2021.
Fertility rates have not rebounded despite the relaxations.

subtopics.title: Reasons for China's Population Decline
subtopics.summary: China's total fertility rate fell to 1.3 births per woman in the 2020 Census, far below the replacement level of 2.1. The One-Child Policy is credited with cutting the TFR from 2.75 in 1979, but fertility did not rebound after later relaxations. Female education, changing family norms, economic pressures and the COVID-19 pandemic are cited as further causes.
facts: TFR declined to 1.3 births per woman (2020 Census), far below the replacement level of 2.1.
The One-Child Policy is credited with reducing TFR from 2.75 (1979) to 1.3 (2020).
Fertility did not rebound after the Two-Child (2016) and Three-Child (2021) relaxations.
The lack of rebound indicates deep-rooted behavioural and socio-economic shifts.
Higher female education and employment have enhanced women's autonomy over reproductive decisions.
Growing disengagement from traditional family structures has reduced pressure to marry early or have many children.
Intense job competition, high urban living costs and work-life imbalance discourage marriage and childbearing.
Housing pressures and economic uncertainty discourage fertility, especially among younger generations.
COVID-19 related mortality and economic uncertainty further accelerated the population decline.
Delayed childbirth and smaller family sizes follow from higher education and employment of women.

subtopics.title: Global and Indian Fertility Context
subtopics.summary: UNFPA's State of World Population 2025 reports a global TFR of 2.25 in 2024, projected to reach the replacement level by 2050. India's fertility rate in 2025 was 1.9, below replacement, with wide regional differences. National schemes such as the National Population Policy 2000, ASHA workers and Janani Suraksha Yojana focus on voluntary choice, institutional deliveries and maternal and child health.
facts: UNFPA was founded in 1969 as the United Nations Fund for Population Activities and renamed in 1987.
Global TFR was 2.25 in 2024 and is projected to hit replacement level of 2.1 by 2050.
Highest TFR: Niger > Somalia > DR Congo; lowest TFR: South Korea < Hong Kong < Singapore.
Elderly (65+) share of population: Japan 30%, Europe 20%, India 7%.
India's fertility rate in 2025 was 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1.
India's working-age population (15-64 years) is 68%.
Above-replacement states: Bihar (2.98) > Meghalaya > UP > Jharkhand > Manipur.
National Population Policy 2000 aimed at replacement-level fertility (TFR 2.1) through voluntary choice.
Janani Suraksha Yojana encourages institutional deliveries and provides free delivery, transport and postnatal care.
Proposal to raise the legal age of marriage for girls to 21 years under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006.

quizzes.passage: A decline in population growth is not explained by one factor alone. The booklet describes it as the result of several forces, and it separates these forces into causes and negative impacts. The causes relate to choices that people make about their careers, their homes and their families, along with the social setting in which those choices are made. Some causes are economic in nature, while others reflect changing attitudes towards family life. The booklet then turns to the consequences of the pattern, which it presents as pressures on several parts of society. These pressures reach the economy, the health sector and the care of people in later life. The booklet also links the pattern to the social and emotional well-being of families. Causes and impacts are set out in the same chapter, so readers can see the reasons behind the decline alongside its effects. Each cause and each impact is presented as a separate point, with its own short explanation in the text. The chapter also includes practice questions on the main figures and terms. The chapter is titled Reports, Summits, Indices and forms part of the January 2026 issue. The booklet uses the term demographic winter for the wider phase in which these causes and impacts appear.

quizzes.passage: China's population has been falling for several years, and the booklet explains this through a set of connected reasons. It first points to a sharp fall in the average number of children per woman, which it describes as far below the level needed to keep a population stable. Earlier government policy forms part of the story, since birth limits were in place for a long period. The booklet also notes that the birth rate did not recover after those limits were loosened, and it treats this as evidence of deeper changes. Social and economic conditions are described as strong influences, including work pressures and the cost of living. The booklet adds that a major public health event and the economic uncertainty that followed it sped up the decline. It also says that the pressures are felt most by younger generations. Taken together, the reasons range from changes in women's lives to the effects of a global health crisis. The booklet also states that these later events accelerated the decline rather than starting it. The phrase used for the broader phase in this chapter is demographic winter, which is discussed in the earlier pages. This section of the January 2026 issue sits within the chapter titled Reports, Summits, Indices.
